A community member independently confirms Unreal "has source code included", and another describes building the engine itself as part of a AAA workflow. The probe shows the GitHub repo is EULA/account-gated rather than public, which is an access caveat, not a contradiction. missing for 10: first-party docs on obtaining, building and modifying the engine source, explicit terms for modifying and distributing engine changes, and hands-on corroboration of patching the engine itself.

Unreal's own docs cover the build-and-export pipeline from the command line. The cook commandlet (`UnrealEditor.exe <uproject> -run=cook -targetplatform=...`) converts content to platform formats. Unreal Automation Tool is described as a generic system for automating building games, and its command can cook, package and deploy a project. Unreal Build Tool configures the executable build. Together these replace clicking through the editor. Missing for 10: explicit documentation of headless/no-UI flags and CI-system integration guidance, and independent hands-on corroboration of CI usage.

Unreal documents a first-party Automation Test Framework for unit, feature and content stress testing, with smoke tests that run when the Editor, game or commandlet starts. It also documents Gauntlet for running engine sessions that execute tests and validate results across platforms, and Unreal Automation Tool as a generic system for automating testing and builds, so in-engine tests can be driven from CI. missing for 10: explicit documentation that tests run with rendering disabled (headless) in CI, a documented CI-integration walkthrough for test runs, independent or hands-on corroboration.

First-party docs cover PBR materials, Lumen as the default fully dynamic global illumination and reflections system, Nanite virtualized geometry, and post-process effects such as depth of field, auto exposure and bloom. Community hands-on reports back this up, describing beautiful lighting and good software-ray-traced results on a GTX 1060. Missing for 10: no explicit documentation of the shadowing system in the evidence pack.

Epic documents packaging and release guides for all supported platforms from one project. These cover one-click deploy to iOS and Android, and Unreal Frontend for deploying to consoles (unreal-supp-platform-targets). The cook commandlet targets multiple platforms at once (-targetplatform=<Plat1>+<Plat2>) and packages content into each platform's native format (unreal-docs-16, unreal-docs-17), and the license grants 'All platforms & features'. Missing for 10: an explicit enumerated list of desktop platforms (Windows/Mac/Linux), documentation of how console SDK and dev-kit access works, and independent hands-on corroboration of one-project multi-platform shipping.

Shipping as an importable, bundleable package is a fair question for a game engine, since some engines are distributed this way, so the axis applies. The evidence shows Unreal Engine is a C++ editor and toolchain compiled with Visual Studio/Xcode and packaged through cook/UAT. Its source is EULA/account-gated, and nothing shows it published to a package registry as an importable or tree-shakeable library. The old HTML5 export mention, editor plugins and the Fab asset marketplace are adjacent features that earn no credit here.

An in-editor AI assistant is a fair capability for a game engine to ship, but the pack documents no official assistant that generates scripts, answers API questions, or scaffolds scenes or assets. The Neural Network Engine (NNE) is only a developer building block for running inference. Python scripting, Remote Control, and llms.txt are automation and machine-readable surfaces, not an assistant, so none of them earn credit.

Epic runs a publicly accessible 'Unreal Engine Public Roadmap' portal with per-release feature entries, which satisfies the story's 'public roadmap I can plan against' option. Governance and funding otherwise remain those of a private company, with no foundation or published finances in evidence. missing for 10: evidence the roadmap is current and forward-looking (the quoted entry is for 5.2), any foundation or published finances, independent corroboration of the roadmap's planning usefulness.

Unreal exposes a broad programmatic surface. Python editor scripting can automate asset tasks, actor placement and import pipelines and drive the editor from custom UIs, backed by a generated per-class API reference. The Remote Control HTTP/WebSocket API can call any Blueprint-callable function, and the CLI and UAT handle cooking, packaging, deploying and testing. Nothing, however, documents true UI parity: the Python API is marked Experimental, and Remote Control reaches only Blueprint-callable or preset-exposed functionality. Missing for 10: an explicit first-party claim or demonstration that every editor UI action is reachable via API, a stable (non-experimental) Python API, and independent hands-on corroboration of parity.

Unreal Engine documents its own import and export of content in glTF, an open Khronos standard, so some project data can leave in an open format. USD is only documented for importing and editing (and is Beta), and FBX is an Autodesk-owned format documented for import. Nothing shows a complete export of a project, such as Blueprints, levels and .uasset content, in open formats. missing for 10: evidence of whole-project export beyond glTF scenes and meshes, a documented open-format export path for Blueprints, maps and other engine-native assets, a stable (non-Beta) USD export, and independent hands-on corroboration of migrating off the engine.

Epic's license page documents 'Access to the source code' for Unreal Engine, and a community comment confirms the engine 'has source code included', so the source can be read. However, the probe found the GitHub repo returns Not Found without credentials because source access is EULA- and account-gated, and nothing in the evidence shows an open license; a community comment calls it 'free neither as beer, or freedom'. missing for 10: source released under an actual open-source license, keyless public access to the repository, first-party documentation of the source license terms.

Unreal Engine is software that runs on the user's own machines. Epic's license grants access to the source code [unreal-docs-10, unreal-docs-18, unreal-docs-21], users compile the engine and editor themselves [unreal-docs-2, unreal-comm-16], and headless dedicated servers can be run on the user's own infrastructure [unreal-supp-dedicated-servers]. Community users corroborate that the source code is included [unreal-comm-6]. Missing for 10: openly accessible source (the GitHub repo is EULA/account-gated and returns Not Found to anonymous clients per unreal-probe-rt-1), explicit first-party documentation framing a fully self-contained/offline self-hosted setup, and independent hands-on corroboration of a fully self-built deployment.

First-party docs cover the core of the story. Unreal Insights is a telemetry capture and analysis suite for performance profiling. MassEntity is a data-oriented, ECS-style gameplay framework with its own debugger, and the Tasks System is a job manager for asynchronous gameplay code built on the TaskGraph scheduler. Nanite's handling of high object counts is related but is not documented instancing. missing for 10: explicit instancing evidence (e.g., instanced static meshes), independent or hands-on corroboration of profiling and scaling in heavy scenes.

The evidence shows a royalty-bearing model, not a royalty-free one. Community reports say Unreal is free only until a game earns $1,000,000, after which payment is owed (unreal-comm-3). One studio estimated Unreal would have cost a $3M-budget game about $150k (unreal-comm-4). The quoted license page lists only source access and 'all platforms & features', with no royalty-free or permissive terms, and source access is EULA/account-gated (unreal-docs-10, unreal-docs-18, unreal-probe-rt-1).

License and pricing stability is a fair question for a commercial game engine, so the axis applies. However, the pack contains no evidence of a track record of stable terms or of any commitment against retroactive repricing of shipped games. The license page snippets only mention source access and platform availability, and the community comments describe current royalty thresholds and costs, not stability over time.

Epic's privacy policy explicitly covers Unreal Engine and describes retention and data-subject rights, so data-residency choice is a fair question for this product. However, nothing in the evidence documents any way to choose a storage region or residency for that data. Retention and access/deletion rights are adjacent privacy controls and earn no credit here.

The axis applies because Epic's privacy policy covers Unreal Engine and its developer tools, so a buyer could fairly ask whether their data is used for AI training. However, the evidence pack documents no AI-training opt-out or no-training commitment. General retention terms and access, correction and deletion rights are adjacent privacy controls, not a training opt-out, so they earn no credit.

Epic's privacy policy explicitly covers Unreal Engine and states that users may have the right to access, correct, or delete personal data collected through Epic Services. That gives a request-based deletion path. Retention, however, is only described as "as long as we reasonably need it," with no user-controllable retention settings. missing for 10: user-configurable retention periods, self-service deletion controls, documentation of what engine/editor data is collected and retained, independent or hands-on corroboration of the deletion process.

Telemetry opt-out is a fair question for a desktop game engine and editor, so the axis applies. The pack contains no documented setting, flag, or config for turning off telemetry or usage tracking. The privacy policy only covers retention and access/correct/delete rights, which is adjacent and not an opt-out. Unreal Insights is a developer profiling tool for your own project, not a vendor usage-tracking control.

Docs show Blueprints exposing "virtually the full range" of programmer concepts, and C++ gameplay classes integrate with the editor through the reflection system and Live Coding, with Visual Studio/Xcode as the toolchain. Community comments note Blueprints become inefficient at scale and push users to C++, which some find unproductive. Missing for 10: any documented script-level debugger (Blueprint breakpoints/stepping or a C++ debugging workflow), evidence that the full engine API is exposed rather than "virtually", and independent corroboration of productivity.

Unreal's official Neural Network Engine (NNE) gives a common API over multiple neural-network runtimes, explicitly for real-time inference inside a game, so the core story is an official first-party capability. NNE is marked Beta ('use caution when shipping with it'), and the evidence is a single overview snippet. Missing for 10: production-ready (non-Beta) status, documentation of supported model formats, runtime backends and target platforms (CPU/GPU, mobile, console), and independent or hands-on corroboration of shipped in-game inference.

Epic's editor scripting docs explicitly list "Create your own Asset import and management pipelines" and automating time-consuming asset tasks such as LOD generation. The Python docs describe building larger-scale asset pipelines that link the editor to other 3D applications, backed by a generated Python API reference, and the FBX/glTF import pipelines give scripts formats to process. missing for 10: documented import hooks/callbacks that fire automatically on incoming assets, documented reusable import presets, hands-on or independent corroboration of batch-import automation.

Epic officially documents generating Python stub files (Developer Mode → Intermediate/PythonStub) with per-IDE setup for autocomplete. A generated per-class Python API reference backs it. Together these are first-party typed API definitions an editor can attach to. They cover only editor Python scripting: the Python API is marked Experimental, stubs require an opt-in setting and editor restart, and nothing comparable is documented for Blueprint gameplay scripting. Missing for 10: an official language server, documented diagnostics/navigation support beyond autocomplete, machine tooling for the primary gameplay scripting path (Blueprints), a non-experimental status, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

First-party docs cover all three named formats. The FBX import pipeline handles meshes, animations, materials and textures, a dedicated page covers glTF import and export, and another covers USD import and editing. USD is flagged as a Beta feature, and nothing in the pack shows that imports are actually 'clean'. Missing for 10: hands-on or independent corroboration of import fidelity, USD out of Beta, and glTF/USD docs detailing which asset types (animation, materials) round-trip.

Epic's Blueprints Visual Scripting docs say designers can use virtually the full range of concepts and tools otherwise available only to programmers, and functions can be defined and implemented entirely in Blueprint. Community users confirm Blueprints work for real logic but note limits: performance suffers as complexity grows, some tasks (vehicles, file/JSON I/O) push users toward C++, and one comment calls them best for prototyping. Missing for 10: in-depth first-party documentation in the pack beyond a single summary line, and independent evidence that complex, production-scale gameplay can be built without any C++.
